question: Can a carefully chosen example break a proposed mathematical rule?
idea: A general rule says something must always happen under particular assumptions. One example satisfying those assumptions but violating the conclusion would overturn the rule. This entry reports such a construction; the exact rule and conditions are stated below.
why: The study of smooth shapes, curvature, and how geometry changes from point to point.

glossary.meaning: A collection of points joined by connections; it can describe a network without requiring a particular drawing.
A shape is convex if the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside the shape.
A bound or statement whose control does not deteriorate across the specified range of inputs.
A single valid object or case that violates a proposed general statement.
The idea that certain constraints force an object to have a very restricted structure.
A description of all objects of a specified kind, usually organized into recognizable types.
A way of measuring the number of independent directions or degrees of freedom; different theories use different notions.

exactClaim: Proves that every smooth locally uniformly convex affine-maximal graph of dimension three through nine, complete for its induced Euclidean metric, is an elliptic paraboloid. A smooth entire nonquadratic example in dimension ten makes this range sharp. In dimensions three through nine, the paraboloid classification also holds for connected open locally uniformly convex affine-maximal hypersurfaces complete for the affine Berwald–Blaschke metric.
scope: A definition-led reading guide; the exact mathematical claim is preserved separately. This is not a proof assessment.
